title: Neural Computation and Brain Networks
summary: How neurons encode information and how large-scale networks coordinate to produce cognition.

lessons.title: Neural Codes: Rate, Timing and Tuning Curves

levels.kid:
Your brain has billions of tiny cells called **neurons**. They talk to each other with quick electric blips called **spikes**. Every spike is the same size, like the same click on a clicker.

So how do neurons send different messages? One way is **how many** clicks they send. Touch your arm lightly and a touch neuron clicks slowly. Press hard and it clicks super fast!

Another way is **when** the clicks happen. A click that comes really early can mean "Something important, right now!"

Each neuron also has a favorite thing, like a favorite song. Its favorite is the thing that makes it click the most. Some neurons in the seeing part of your brain love lines that tilt one way. Scientists draw a graph of what a neuron likes. It is called a **tuning curve**.
levels.hs:
Neurons communicate with **action potentials**, also called **spikes**. These are brief electrical pulses lasting about 1 millisecond. A spike is **all-or-none**: it either fires fully or not at all, and spikes from the same neuron look almost identical. So information is not carried in spike size. It is carried in the pattern of spikes, called the **neural code**.

- **Rate code**: information is in the **firing rate**, the number of spikes per second. In 1926 Edgar Adrian and Yngve Zotterman recorded from a stretch receptor in a frog muscle. Heavier weights made it fire faster, not produce bigger spikes. Adrian shared the 1932 Nobel Prize partly for this work.
- **Temporal code**: information is in exactly **when** spikes occur, for example how soon the first spike arrives after a stimulus, or whether spikes line up with a brain rhythm.

A **tuning curve** is a graph of a neuron's firing rate plotted against one feature of a stimulus. Its peak marks the neuron's **preferred stimulus**. In 1959 David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel showed cats bars of light and found that many neurons in primary visual cortex (V1) fire strongly for an edge at one orientation and less as the bar rotates away. That tuning curve is a hill centered on the favorite angle.

Real brains use both rate and timing, depending on the job.
levels.college:
**Rate coding.** Firing rate can be measured as a spike count in a time window, or as a **peri-stimulus time histogram (PSTH)**, which averages spikes across repeated trials in small time bins to show how rate changes moment to moment. Cortical neurons range from near 0 to a few hundred spikes per second; the refractory period caps the maximum. A major complication is **variability**: the same stimulus shown repeatedly gives different spike counts, with variance roughly equal to the mean, as in a **Poisson process**. Reading a rate reliably needs either time or many neurons.

**Temporal coding** uses information in spike timing:
- **Latency**: stronger or more salient stimuli trigger earlier first spikes.
- **Phase-locking**: auditory nerve fibers fire at a consistent point in each sound-wave cycle, up to roughly 4 kHz in mammals.
- **Phase precession**: O'Keefe and Recce (1993) found that rat hippocampal **place cells** fire at progressively earlier points of each **theta** cycle (about 6-10 Hz) as the animal crosses the cell's place field, so timing adds position information beyond rate.
- **Precision**: Mainen and Sejnowski (1995) found that a constant current step gave spike times that drifted across trials, while a rapidly fluctuating, noise-like input produced spikes repeatable to about a millisecond.

**Tuning curves** summarize selectivity:
- **Bell-shaped (Gaussian or von Mises)**: V1 orientation tuning, described by preferred value, peak rate, baseline and **bandwidth**.
- **Cosine**: Georgopoulos and colleagues (1982) found monkey motor cortex neurons fire most for arm movements in one direction, falling off roughly as the cosine of the angle from it.
- **Monotonic (sigmoid)**: rate rises with intensity, as in many stretch and touch receptors.
- **Spatial**: place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971) are tuned to location.

One tuning curve is ambiguous: a given rate matches stimuli on either side of the peak, which is why the brain reads many neurons together.
levels.phd:
**Rate versus timing is a question of timescale.** Any spike train becomes a rate if you bin finely enough; the real issue is whether downstream neurons read millisecond patterns or integrate over tens to hundreds of milliseconds. Softky and Koch (1993) argued that cortical irregularity (interspike-interval coefficient of variation near 1) is hard to explain if neurons simply integrate many inputs, implying coincidence detection. Shadlen and Newsome (1994, 1998) countered that balanced excitation and inhibition naturally yields Poisson-like irregularity, making individual spike times largely noise and favoring population rate codes. The **Fano factor** (count variance/mean) is near 1 but falls at stimulus onset (Churchland et al., 2010), so variability is itself state dependent.

**Information theory.** Bialek, Rieke, de Ruyter van Steveninck and colleagues decoded stimuli from the fly H1 motion neuron and found information on the order of one to a few bits per spike, near limits set by timing precision (*Spikes*, 1997).

**Speed arguments.** Thorpe, Fize and Marlot (1996) found EEG differences between animal and non-animal scenes by about 150 ms. With roughly ten synaptic stages from retina to inferotemporal cortex, each stage has time for about one spike per neuron, too few to estimate a rate, motivating latency and rank-order codes. Johansson and Birznieks (2004) showed that relative first-spike latencies of human fingertip afferents signal force direction and surface curvature faster than rates could.

**Microsecond codes.** Barn owls locate prey by **interaural time differences** resolved to about 10 microseconds in nucleus laminaris, implementing Jeffress's 1948 model of axonal delay lines feeding coincidence detectors. Mammals may rely more on precisely timed inhibition in the medial superior olive.

**Tuning curves and Fisher information.** Discrimination depends on tuning-curve slope relative to noise. For a Poisson neuron, Fisher information is proportional to f'(s)²/f(s): zero at the peak, maximal on the steep **flank**. So the best neuron for telling two nearby orientations apart is not the one that prefers them. Britten et al. (1992) found single MT neurons' **neurometric** sensitivity to motion direction often matched the monkey's **psychometric** performance.
levels.expert:
**Tuning curves are not fixed.** McAdams and Maunsell (1999) showed that attention multiplicatively scales V4 orientation tuning curves, raising their height by roughly a quarter without shifting the preferred orientation or changing bandwidth. Treue and Martinez-Trujillo (1999) extended this to feature-similarity gain in MT. Adaptation can produce repulsive shifts, moving preferred orientation away from an adapting stimulus (Dragoi et al., 2000).

**Pharmacology of selectivity.** Sillito (1975) applied the GABA-A antagonist bicuculline iontophoretically in cat V1 and reduced orientation and direction selectivity, implicating intracortical inhibition in sharpening tuning. Ferster's intracellular recordings later showed excitatory input is already substantially tuned, so the current view combines feedforward Hubel-Wiesel wiring with inhibition that maintains contrast-invariant tuning; the balance remains debated. Herrero et al. (2008) found that blocking muscarinic receptors with scopolamine reduced attentional modulation in macaque V1, linking acetylcholine to rate-gain control.

**Methodological pitfalls.**
- Spike-sorting errors that merge units produce artificially broad tuning.
- Calcium indicators such as GCaMP have kinetics of tens to hundreds of milliseconds, so imaging reports a smoothed rate and largely discards spike timing; deconvolution recovers spikes imperfectly.
- Electrodes oversample large, active neurons, under-representing sparse firers.

**Timing matters for learning.** Spike-timing-dependent plasticity (Markram et al., 1997; Bi and Poo, 1998) potentiates or depresses synapses depending on pre/post order within about 20 ms, so timing shapes circuits even where readout is rate-based.

**Clinical translation.**
- **Brain-computer interfaces**: BrainGate (Hochberg et al., 2006, 2012) decoded intended movement from directionally tuned motor cortex neurons; tuning drifts across days, requiring recalibration.
- **Cochlear implants** convey mainly envelope and place cues; pitch from electrical stimulation rate typically saturates around 300 Hz, limiting music and tonal-language perception.
- **DBS surgery**: intraoperative microelectrode recording identifies subthalamic nucleus by its high, irregular firing and beta-range bursting, and maps motor territory by neurons responding to passive joint movement.

**Open questions**: how much downstream circuits read timing versus rate, and how silent or sparsely firing neurons contribute.

keyPoints: Spikes are all-or-none, so information lies in spike patterns
Rate codes use spikes per unit time; Adrian showed stronger stimuli raise firing rate
Temporal codes use latency, phase-locking and phase precession
A tuning curve plots firing rate against a stimulus feature; its peak is the preferred stimulus
Fine discrimination is best on the steep flank of a tuning curve, not the peak
Tuning is modulated by attention, inhibition and neuromodulators like acetylcholine

test.q: What does a rate code use to carry information?
choices: The number of spikes per unit time
The height of each action potential
The type of neurotransmitter released
The diameter of the axon
test.explain: A rate code reads how many spikes occur in a time window. Spike height carries little information because spikes are all-or-none.

test.q: Adrian and Zotterman found that heavier weights on a frog muscle stretch receptor produced:
choices: Longer refractory periods
Higher firing rates
Larger action potentials
Slower conduction speed
test.explain: Stimulus strength was signaled by faster firing, not bigger spikes, the founding observation of rate coding.

test.q: A tuning curve plots:
choices: Synaptic strength against time since learning
Spike timing against the theta rhythm
Membrane voltage over one millisecond
Firing rate against a stimulus feature
test.explain: A tuning curve shows how a neuron's firing rate changes as one stimulus feature, such as orientation or direction, varies.

test.q: Hubel and Wiesel found that many cat V1 neurons respond best to:
choices: Uniform changes in brightness
Edges at one orientation
Pure tones of one pitch
Faces of familiar animals
test.explain: V1 neurons are orientation tuned, firing most for an edge or bar at a preferred angle.

test.q: Phase precession in hippocampal place cells means:
choices: The place field drifts to a new location each day
Firing rate doubles each time the animal enters the field
Spikes fire earlier in each theta cycle across the field
Spikes lock to the peak of each gamma cycle
test.explain: O'Keefe and Recce showed spikes move to progressively earlier points of the theta cycle as the rat crosses the field, so timing carries position information.

test.q: Where did Georgopoulos find arm-movement direction tuning that is roughly cosine-shaped?
choices: Motor cortex neurons
Cerebellar Purkinje cells
Primary auditory cortex
Retinal ganglion cells
test.explain: Monkey motor cortex neurons fire most for one movement direction, falling off roughly as the cosine of the angle from it.

test.q: Barn owls locate prey in the dark mainly by computing:
choices: Echoes returning from their own high-pitched calls
The overall firing rate of their optic nerve fibers
Tiny differences in when sound reaches each ear
Shifts in the brightness of reflected moonlight
test.explain: Barn owls use interaural time differences resolved to about 10 microseconds, computed by coincidence detectors in nucleus laminaris. They do not echolocate.

test.q: Cortical spike counts to repeated identical stimuli are typically:
choices: Steadily rising with each repetition
Variable, variance close to the mean
Silent after the first presentation
Nearly identical from trial to trial
test.explain: Cortical responses are Poisson-like, with count variance roughly equal to the mean, so rates must be estimated over time or many neurons.

test.q: Mainen and Sejnowski found a cortical neuron's spike timing was most repeatable across trials when driven by:
choices: A slowly rising current ramp
A steady hyperpolarizing step
A rapidly fluctuating input
A constant step of current
test.explain: Fluctuating, noise-like input produced spikes repeatable to about a millisecond, while a constant step gave drifting spike times.

test.q: The stimulus that makes a neuron fire fastest is its ___ stimulus.
test.explain: The peak of the tuning curve marks the preferred stimulus.

test.q: What is the all-or-none electrical pulse neurons use to signal, also called a spike?
test.explain: Action potentials are brief, roughly 1 ms, all-or-none pulses.

test.q: Auditory nerve fibers that fire at a consistent point in each sound-wave cycle show phase-___.
test.explain: Phase-locking preserves the timing of the sound wave, up to roughly 4 kHz in mammals.

kidTest.q: How do neurons send messages to each other?
choices: With tiny electric spikes
With bright flashes of light
With quiet humming sounds
kidTest.explain: Neurons talk with quick electric blips called spikes.

kidTest.q: When you press harder on your arm, your touch neurons:
choices: Send spikes faster
Make bigger spikes
Stop sending spikes
kidTest.explain: Spikes stay the same size, but more of them come each second when the press is stronger.

kidTest.q: A neuron's favorite thing is the thing that makes it:
choices: Fire the most
Stop firing
Grow much longer
kidTest.explain: A neuron's favorite is what makes it click the most.

kidTest.q: Besides how many spikes, what else can carry a message?
choices: How wide the neuron is
How warm the neuron is
When the spikes happen
kidTest.explain: The timing of spikes matters too. An early spike can mean something important is happening now.

kidTest.q: The graph of what a neuron likes best is called a tuning c _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: A tuning curve shows how much a neuron fires for different things.

advancedTest.q: Under a Fisher-information analysis with Poisson noise, a neuron best discriminates two nearby orientations when they fall:
choices: Far out in the flat tails
At the peak of the tuning curve
At the baseline firing rate level
On the steep flank of the curve
advancedTest.explain: Fisher information scales with f'(s)²/f(s), which is zero at the peak where the slope is flat. Small stimulus changes alter rate most on the steep flank.

advancedTest.q: Humans categorize scenes by about 150 ms through roughly ten processing stages. Why does this challenge a single-neuron rate code?
choices: Gamma oscillations are too slow to synchronize the stages
Each stage allows roughly one spike per neuron to be read
Rate codes require feedback from prefrontal cortex first
Axonal conduction is too slow to cross ten synaptic stages
advancedTest.explain: With about 10-15 ms per stage, a neuron can fire about one spike, too few to estimate a rate, which motivated latency and rank-order codes.

advancedTest.q: McAdams and Maunsell found attention scales V4 orientation tuning curves multiplicatively. What happens to the curve's shape?
choices: Width and peak position stay about the same as height rises
Preferred orientation shifts toward the attended one
Bandwidth narrows sharply while height is unchanged
The curve flattens into nonselective firing
advancedTest.explain: Multiplicative gain raises responses proportionally, increasing height without moving the preferred orientation or changing bandwidth.

advancedTest.q: Blocking GABA-A receptors with bicuculline in cat V1 reduces orientation selectivity. The best inference is:
choices: Intracortical inhibition helps sharpen the tuning
GABA acts as the main excitatory transmitter in V1
Bicuculline works by silencing V1 neuron firing
Orientation selectivity arises in the retina itself
advancedTest.explain: Removing inhibition broadened tuning, so inhibition contributes to sharpening it. Intracellular work shows excitatory input is already partly tuned, so both mechanisms matter.

lessons.title: Population Coding and Neural Manifolds

levels.kid:
Imagine a choir singing one song. One singer alone might be quiet or a little off-key. But when many singers sing together, you hear the song clearly. Your brain works the same way.

Each brain cell, called a **neuron**, gives a small "vote" about what is happening. Some neurons like it when your arm moves left. Others like it when your arm moves right. The brain listens to the whole crowd and adds up the votes. This is called **population coding**.

Scientists can now listen to thousands of neurons at once. They found a surprise. The crowd's activity does not jump around randomly. It moves along neat paths, like a train on hidden tracks. These tracks are called **neural manifolds**. Learning a new move is easier when the brain can stay on its usual tracks.
levels.hs:
A single neuron is a noisy messenger. Its **firing rate** (spikes per second) changes from trial to trial even when the stimulus is identical. So the brain rarely relies on one cell. Instead it uses **population coding**: information is spread across many neurons, each giving partial, overlapping clues.

The classic example comes from Apostolos Georgopoulos in the 1980s. He recorded neurons in the **motor cortex** of monkeys reaching in different directions. Each neuron fired most for one **preferred direction** and less for others, so its tuning was broad. No single neuron could specify the reach. But when he let every neuron "vote" for its preferred direction, weighted by how strongly it fired, the sum of the votes, called the **population vector**, pointed almost exactly where the arm went.

Why spread information out?
- **Robustness**: losing a few neurons barely changes the answer.
- **Averaging**: random noise in individual cells partly cancels out.
- **Precision**: many broadly tuned cells together can signal fine differences.

Today, electrode arrays record hundreds to thousands of neurons at once. When scientists plot all that activity together, it doesn't wander everywhere. It stays on a much simpler surface called a **neural manifold**, like a path through a huge space. These patterns are what **brain-computer interfaces** read to let paralyzed people move cursors or robotic arms.
levels.college:
**From tuning curves to populations.** Many cortical neurons are broadly tuned. In motor cortex, Georgopoulos found approximately **cosine tuning**: firing rate ≈ baseline + gain × cos(θ − θpref), where θ is reach direction and θpref is the cell's preferred direction. Because each curve is broad, many cells respond to any movement, and each response alone is ambiguous.

**Decoding.** A decoder reads the population to estimate a variable:
- **Population vector**: sum each cell's preferred-direction vector weighted by its baseline-subtracted rate. Simple, but biased if preferred directions are unevenly distributed.
- **Optimal linear estimators** and **Kalman filters** learn weights from data and correct those biases; Kalman filters drove many clinical BCIs.
- **Bayesian decoders** compute the most probable stimulus given the spikes plus each cell's tuning and noise.

**Noise correlations.** Pooling helps most when neurons' trial-to-trial noise is independent. Zohary, Newsome and Shadlen (1994) found that neurons in visual area MT share weakly correlated noise (average r ≈ 0.1 to 0.2). Even this small correlation means accuracy saturates after pooling roughly 50 to 100 neurons, because shared noise does not average away.

**State space and manifolds.** Record N neurons and each moment becomes a point in an N-dimensional **state space** (one axis per neuron's firing rate); over time the point traces a **neural trajectory**. Because neurons are interconnected, trajectories occupy a far lower-dimensional region, the **neural manifold**. Dimensionality reduction reveals it:
- **PCA** finds the axes of greatest variance.
- **Factor analysis** and **GPFA** separate shared variability from private, single-neuron noise.
- Nonlinear methods (Isomap, UMAP, autoencoders) capture curved manifolds.

**Examples.** Head-direction cells collectively trace a **ring**, matching the circular variable they encode. Motor cortex activity during reaching follows smooth, low-dimensional trajectories rather than random fluctuations.

The key shift: the meaningful unit of computation may be the population's pattern and its dynamics, not any single neuron.
levels.phd:
**Information in populations.** Coding precision is quantified with **Fisher information** I(θ), which bounds the variance of any unbiased estimator (Cramér-Rao: var ≥ 1/I). For independent Poisson neurons, I grows linearly with N, and each cell contributes most on the steep flanks of its tuning curve, not at its peak. Correlations change this. Moreno-Bote et al. (2014) showed that **differential correlations**, noise aligned with f′(θ) (the direction the mean response moves as θ changes), are what cap information, because they are indistinguishable from a real change in the stimulus. Other correlation structures can be harmless or even beneficial. The question is not "how correlated?" but "correlated along which axis?"

**Mixed selectivity.** Many prefrontal neurons respond to nonlinear conjunctions of task variables. Rigotti et al. (2013) showed that **nonlinear mixed selectivity** raises population dimensionality, letting a linear readout separate many task conditions; dimensionality collapsed on error trials.

**Computation through dynamics.** Shenoy, Sahani and Churchland framed motor cortex as a dynamical system. Churchland et al. (2012) used jPCA to reveal **rotational dynamics** during reaching. Kaufman et al. (2014) showed that preparatory activity occupies an **output-null subspace**, varying along dimensions the muscle readout ignores, then moves into **output-potent** dimensions at movement onset. This explains how cortex prepares without moving.

**Manifolds constrain learning.** Sadtler et al. (2014) built BCIs mapping M1 activity to cursor velocity through a roughly 10-dimensional **intrinsic manifold** identified with factor analysis. Monkeys quickly learned perturbed mappings that stayed within the manifold but largely failed at mappings that required patterns outside it.

**Topology.** Using topological data analysis, Chaudhuri et al. (2019) showed that head-direction population activity lies on a ring that persists in sleep. Gardner et al. (2022) found that grid-cell module activity lies on a **torus**, also preserved in sleep, consistent with continuous attractor networks.

**Low or high dimensional?** Stringer et al. (2019), recording about 10,000 V1 neurons, found variance spectra following a power law with exponent near 1: high-dimensional, yet as high as possible while staying smooth. Reported low dimensionality may partly reflect simple tasks.
levels.expert:
**BCIs as applied population coding.** Intracortical Utah arrays, implanted by neurosurgeons into motor cortex, sample roughly 100 to 200 channels, a tiny fraction of the population. They suffice because behaviorally relevant activity is low-dimensional and redundantly expressed. Milestones: Willett et al. (2021) decoded attempted handwriting at about 90 characters per minute; in 2023, Willett et al. (intracortical) and Metzger et al. (high-density ECoG) decoded attempted speech at roughly 62 and 78 words per minute. Modern decoders are recurrent networks paired with language models, not population vectors.

**The stability problem.** Electrodes micro-move, units drop out, and single-neuron identity changes over days, so decoders degrade and need recalibration. The manifold view offers a fix: Gallego et al. (2020) showed that latent dynamics for a behavior remain stable for up to two years while recorded neurons change, and can be realigned with canonical correlation analysis. Unsupervised alignment aims to spare patients repeated calibration sessions.

**Analysis pitfalls.**
- Trial-averaging and smoothing can manufacture structure. Elsayed and Cunningham (2017) introduced tensor maximum entropy surrogates to test whether structure exceeds what tuning and temporal smoothness predict; rotations survived, and such controls are now expected. Lebedev et al. (2019) argued that rotations can arise from simple sequential firing.
- Measured dimensionality is bounded by **task complexity** (Gao and Ganguli): simple tasks yield low-dimensional data almost by construction.
- "Manifold" is often used loosely for a linear subspace; PCA overestimates the dimension of curved manifolds.
- **Representational drift**: in hippocampus and posterior parietal cortex, single-cell tuning changes across days while behavior and population decodability persist.

**Neuromodulation.** Attention reduces noise correlations in V4 (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009), and that decorrelation explains much of attention's perceptual benefit. Cholinergic and noradrenergic systems are leading candidates for setting population state, a natural target for cognitive pharmacology.

**Open questions.** Neuropixels probes and two-photon imaging capture thousands of neurons; latent-variable models such as LFADS and CEBRA infer single-trial dynamics. Unresolved: how areas communicate through low-dimensional **communication subspaces** (Semedo et al., 2019), and whether neurological and psychiatric disorders reflect distorted manifold geometry.

keyPoints: Population coding spreads information across many broadly tuned, noisy neurons
Georgopoulos's population vector predicted reach direction from motor cortex activity
Shared noise correlations limit how much pooling neurons improves accuracy
Population activity occupies low-dimensional neural manifolds in state space
Manifold structure constrains learning and stays stable as single neurons change
Brain-computer interfaces decode population patterns to restore movement and speech

test.q: What does population coding mean?
choices: Information carried by the speed of one axon
Information stored in a single synapse's strength
Information carried by one highly selective neuron
Information spread across many neurons' activity
test.explain: In population coding, many neurons each give partial, overlapping clues, and the pattern across the group carries the message.

test.q: In Georgopoulos's experiments, the population vector closely matched:
choices: The speed of the eye movement
The color of the visual target
The direction the arm moved
The force of the muscle pull
test.explain: Summing each motor cortex neuron's preferred direction, weighted by its firing, produced a vector pointing almost exactly where the arm reached.

choices: Narrow tuning to one exact angle
No preference among directions
Tuning to movement timing instead
Broad tuning around a preference
test.explain: Motor cortex neurons are broadly (roughly cosine) tuned around a preferred direction, so each responds to many movements.

test.q: Why does pooling more and more neurons improve accuracy less than expected?
choices: Correlated noise fails to average out
Tuning curves are too narrow to overlap
Downstream areas ignore most inputs
Neurons fire too slowly to be summed
test.explain: Zohary and colleagues showed that even weak shared noise between neurons does not cancel when pooled, so accuracy saturates.

test.q: In a population state space, each axis represents:
choices: One stimulus feature
One neuron's firing rate
One brain region's volume
One moment in time
test.explain: With N recorded neurons, each axis is one neuron's rate, and each moment of activity is a single point in that space.

test.q: The low-dimensional region of state space where population activity tends to stay is called a:
choices: Receptive field
Tuning curve
Neural manifold
Cortical column
test.explain: A neural manifold is the lower-dimensional surface that coordinated population activity occupies. A tuning curve describes one neuron, not the population.

test.q: Which method finds the axes along which population activity varies the most?
choices: Spike sorting
PCA
Fourier transform
Patch clamp
test.explain: Principal component analysis (PCA) finds the directions of greatest variance and is a standard way to reveal manifolds.

test.q: Head-direction cells, analyzed together, trace which shape in state space?
choices: A spiral
A ring
A sphere
A straight line
test.explain: Heading is a circular variable, and head-direction population activity lies on a ring that matches it.

test.q: Brain-computer interfaces that let paralyzed people move cursors mainly work by:
choices: Measuring blood flow in the spinal cord
Decoding many motor cortex neurons
Stimulating arm muscles with electrodes
Reading a single neuron for each finger
test.explain: BCIs decode the activity pattern of many motor cortex neurons, exploiting population coding, rather than relying on single cells.

test.q: Georgopoulos found motor cortex neurons follow approximately ___ tuning, firing most for a preferred direction.
test.explain: Firing rate ≈ baseline + gain × cos(θ − θpref), a broad tuning curve.

test.q: What is the name for the sum of each neuron's preferred-direction 'vote', weighted by how strongly it fires?
test.explain: The population vector was Georgopoulos's simple decoder for reach direction.

test.q: Trial-to-trial variability that is shared between neurons is called noise ___.
test.explain: Noise correlations are shared fluctuations; depending on their structure, they can limit population information.

kidTest.q: What is population coding?
choices: Neurons taking turns sleeping
One big neuron doing the whole job
Many neurons sharing one message
kidTest.explain: Lots of neurons each give a little vote, and the brain adds them up.

choices: Neurons are too tiny to work
A crowd uses less energy
One neuron alone can be wrong
kidTest.explain: One neuron can make mistakes, but many together give a clearer answer.

A big empty hall
Many voices together
kidTest.explain: Just like neurons, many singers together make the message easy to hear.

kidTest.q: What are the hidden 'tracks' that brain activity moves along called?

Manifolds

kidTest.q: Each brain cell is called a n _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Neurons are the brain cells that send signals and vote together.

advancedTest.q: According to Moreno-Bote et al. (2014), which noise correlations fundamentally limit the information a large population carries about θ?
choices: Any positive pairwise correlation, whatever its axis
Correlations among cells with opposite preferences
Noise confined to dimensions orthogonal to f′(θ)
Noise aligned with how mean responses shift with θ
advancedTest.explain: Differential correlations along f′(θ) mimic a real stimulus change, so no decoder can remove them. Noise orthogonal to f′(θ) can be ignored by an optimal readout.

advancedTest.q: Motor cortex shows strong preparatory activity before a reach, yet the arm stays still. Population analyses best explain this by showing that preparatory activity:
choices: Is suppressed by spinal inhibition before reaching muscles
Is too weak in firing rate to drive motoneurons
Occurs in neurons lacking projections to the spinal cord
Lies in dimensions the muscle readout does not weight
advancedTest.explain: Kaufman et al. showed that preparatory activity occupies an output-null subspace, then shifts into output-potent dimensions at movement onset.

advancedTest.q: In Sadtler et al.'s BCI study, monkeys adapted quickly to some decoder perturbations but not others. What predicted success?
choices: Whether the cursor moved faster than under the old mapping
Whether the perturbation was introduced gradually over days
Whether needed patterns lay within the intrinsic manifold
Whether the recorded neurons had strong cosine tuning
advancedTest.explain: Within-manifold perturbations could be learned by reusing existing activity patterns. Outside-manifold mappings required new patterns and were largely not learned.

advancedTest.q: A lab finds motor cortex activity in a simple two-target task is 3-dimensional and concludes that cortex is intrinsically low-dimensional. The strongest critique is that:
choices: Measured dimensionality is bounded by task complexity
Three dimensions match the three joints of the arm
Motor cortex has too few neurons for more dimensions
PCA overestimates dimensionality in small datasets
advancedTest.explain: Gao and Ganguli argued that simple tasks yield low-dimensional data almost by construction. Stringer et al. found high-dimensional V1 responses when stimuli were rich.

lessons.title: Brain Rhythms: Theta, Alpha, Beta and Gamma Oscillations

levels.kid:
Your brain has billions of nerve cells that send tiny electric signals. Sometimes lots of them fire together, again and again, like a crowd clapping in time. These steady beats are called **brain waves**.

Brain waves come in different speeds, like slow drums and fast drums:
- Calm waves called **alpha** show up when you close your eyes and relax.
- Fast waves called **gamma** show up when you focus hard on something.
- **Theta** waves help you remember places, like the way to your friend's house.
- **Beta** waves help you hold still or get ready to move.

Each beat works like a drummer in a band. It helps different parts of the brain keep time together.

Doctors can listen to these beats with little stickers on your head. This test is called an **EEG**, and it doesn't hurt!
levels.hs:
A **brain oscillation** (or brain rhythm) is a repeating rise and fall in electrical activity. It appears when large groups of neurons become active together. One neuron's signal is far too tiny to detect through the skull. But when thousands of neurons receive inputs in sync, their currents add up. An **EEG** (electroencephalogram) picks up these summed signals with electrodes on the scalp.

Rhythms are named by their **frequency**, measured in hertz (Hz, cycles per second):
- **Delta** (1-4 Hz): deep sleep.
- **Theta** (4-8 Hz): memory and navigation; strong in the hippocampus.
- **Alpha** (8-12 Hz): relaxed wakefulness, strongest over the back of the head with eyes closed.
- **Beta** (13-30 Hz): movement control and holding a position steady.
- **Gamma** (30-100 Hz): active processing and focused attention.

A real example: in 1929 the German psychiatrist **Hans Berger** published the first human EEG. He saw a large rhythm of about 10 Hz when people closed their eyes, and it shrank as soon as they opened them. We still call this the alpha rhythm. Its blocking by eye opening is still checked in routine EEGs today.

Why do rhythms matter? A rhythm acts like a shared clock. Neurons that fire at the same point in a wave are more likely to influence one another, so rhythms help brain areas coordinate. Faster rhythms tend to organize small local circuits. Slower rhythms can link distant regions.
levels.college:
Oscillations recorded as **local field potentials (LFP)** or EEG mostly reflect synchronized synaptic currents, not spikes. The biggest contribution comes from pyramidal cells, which are lined up in parallel. The rhythm itself comes from three main sources: interactions between excitatory and inhibitory neurons, the intrinsic properties of cell membranes, and loops between the thalamus and cortex.

How each band is generated and what it does:
- **Gamma (30-100 Hz)**: In the **PING** (pyramidal-interneuron network gamma) model, pyramidal cells excite **parvalbumin (PV) fast-spiking basket cells**. These cells inhibit the pyramidal cells back through GABA-A receptors. As the inhibition decays over a few milliseconds, a window opens for the next cycle. Gamma rises locally when a region processes a stimulus, as in visual cortex during viewing.
- **Theta (4-8 Hz in humans; about 6-10 Hz in rodent hippocampus)**: Paced by the **medial septum**, which projects to the hippocampus. Rodent hippocampal theta dominates during running and exploration. In humans, **frontal midline theta** rises with working-memory load and when conflict or errors demand control.
- **Alpha (8-12 Hz)**: Generated in thalamocortical circuits, and stronger over disengaged regions. When you attend to the left visual field, alpha increases over left occipital cortex, which processes the ignored right side. This supports the view of alpha as **functional inhibition**.
- **Beta (13-30 Hz)**: Prominent in sensorimotor cortex and basal ganglia. Beta power drops before and during movement (**event-related desynchronization**). After the movement stops, it rises above baseline (**post-movement beta rebound**). Beta is linked to maintaining the current motor or cognitive state.

**Cross-frequency coupling**: Rhythms interact. In the hippocampus, gamma bursts ride on particular phases of theta (**theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling**). This is a candidate mechanism for organizing sequences of items.

**Clinical link**: In Parkinson's disease, dopamine loss produces excessive beta synchrony in the **subthalamic nucleus (STN)** and cortex. This beta correlates with slowness and rigidity, and it decreases with dopamine-replacement therapy.
levels.phd:
Oscillations are best treated as dynamical regimes of excitation-inhibition (E-I) circuits. The central question is which rhythms are causal for computation and which are byproducts.

**Gamma.** Two models dominate:
- **PING**: pyramidal bursts recruit PV interneurons, and their GABA-A inhibition sets the period.
- **ING**: mutually coupled interneurons generate the rhythm alone.

Cardin et al. (2009) drove PV cells optogenetically and selectively amplified gamma. Sohal et al. (2009) showed that gamma enhanced information transmission in cortical circuits. Gray and Singer's (1989) stimulus-specific gamma synchrony in cat visual cortex inspired the **binding-by-synchrony** hypothesis. Ray and Maunsell (2010) undercut it: gamma peak frequency in V1 shifts with stimulus contrast, so parts of one object at different contrasts would not share a common clock. Fries's **communication-through-coherence** hypothesis proposes instead that phase alignment between areas gates effective connectivity. Bastos et al. (2015) found that in macaque visual cortex, feedforward influences travel mainly in theta and gamma, and feedback in alpha-beta.

**Theta.** O'Keefe and Recce (1993) discovered **phase precession**: a place cell fires at progressively earlier theta phases as the animal crosses its field. This compresses behavioral sequences into cycles of roughly 100 ms. Lisman and Idiart (1995) proposed that each working-memory item occupies one gamma cycle nested within a theta cycle. Capacity would then be set by the gamma-to-theta ratio, roughly seven. Canolty et al. (2006) demonstrated theta-high gamma coupling in human ECoG.

**Alpha and beta.** The **gating-by-inhibition** framework (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010) treats alpha as pulsed inhibition. Prestimulus alpha phase and power predict whether near-threshold stimuli are detected. Engel and Fries (2010) proposed that beta signals maintenance of the **status quo**. Shin et al. (2017) showed that neocortical beta occurs as brief bursts of about 150 ms. Burst rate and timing, not sustained amplitude, predicted tactile detection. Trial averaging smears these bursts into an apparently sustained rhythm.

**Method caveat.** Power spectra contain an **aperiodic 1/f component**. Tools such as specparam (formerly FOOOF; Donoghue et al., 2020) separate it from true oscillatory peaks. A band-power increase without a spectral peak may reflect a broadband aperiodic shift, not a rhythm. The aperiodic exponent has been proposed to track E-I balance (Gao et al., 2017).
levels.expert:
For a clinician-scientist, rhythms are biomarkers, therapeutic targets and frequent sources of artifact.

**Intracranial recordings.** Much human oscillation data comes from neurosurgical epilepsy patients monitored with stereo-EEG or ECoG. In these recordings, broadband **high gamma (about 70-150 Hz)** is best read as a proxy for local population spiking, not a true oscillation. It supports passive mapping of language and motor cortex alongside electrical stimulation mapping.

**Deep brain stimulation.** Exaggerated STN beta helps confirm the dorsolateral sensorimotor STN during lead placement. **Adaptive (closed-loop) DBS** adjusts stimulation according to sensed STN beta; Medtronic's BrainSense Adaptive system gained European and US approval in 2025. It has limits:
- Beta is weak in some patients.
- It tracks bradykinesia and rigidity better than tremor.
- It must be sensed amid stimulation artifact.

Cole, Voytek and colleagues showed that Parkinsonian beta waves are sharp and asymmetric. Waveform shape carries information that Fourier-based measures miss.

**Psychiatry and pharmacology.** Schizophrenia shows a reduced **40 Hz auditory steady-state response**, linked to PV interneuron and NMDA receptor dysfunction. Paradoxically, the NMDA antagonist ketamine increases resting gamma power, probably by disinhibiting pyramidal cells. Pharmaco-EEG signatures are robust. Benzodiazepines (GABA-A positive allosteric modulators) raise beta power. Propofol produces frontal alpha (anteriorization), which is used in anesthetic monitoring.

**40 Hz stimulation.** Iaccarino et al. (2016) reported that 40 Hz flicker reduced amyloid in Alzheimer's mouse models (the GENUS approach). Soula et al. (2023) found neither deep entrainment nor amyloid reduction. Human trials continue, and efficacy remains unsettled.

**Pitfalls.**
- Microsaccades generate scalp induced gamma (Yuval-Greenberg et al., 2008), and muscle (EMG) contamination inflates beta and gamma.
- Volume conduction and reference choice create spurious EEG coherence. Source-level or lag-based measures, such as imaginary coherence, help.
- Filtering non-sinusoidal waves creates harmonics and false phase-amplitude coupling.
- In **tACS**, much of the current is shunted by the scalp (Vöröslakos et al., 2018), so some reported effects may act through peripheral nerves.

**Open question.** Are rhythms causal or epiphenomenal? Closed-loop, phase-locked perturbation offers the cleanest test. One example is auditory stimulation timed to sleep slow waves, which enhanced memory (Ngo et al., 2013).

keyPoints: Oscillations are synchronized synaptic currents summed across many neurons, seen in EEG and LFP
Bands: theta 4-8, alpha 8-12, beta 13-30, gamma 30-100 Hz
Gamma arises from pyramidal-PV interneuron loops and marks active local processing
Hippocampal theta, paced by the medial septum, organizes memory and navigation
Alpha acts as functional inhibition; beta maintains the current motor state
Excess STN beta in Parkinson's is now used to steer adaptive deep brain stimulation

test.q: Which frequency range defines the alpha band?
choices: 4-8 Hz
test.explain: Alpha is 8-12 Hz. The 4-8 Hz range is theta, 13-30 Hz is beta, and 30-100 Hz is gamma.

Cholinergic neurons of the medial septum
Parvalbumin fast-spiking basket cells
Purkinje cells of the cerebellum
test.explain: In PING, pyramidal cells excite PV basket cells, and their GABA-A inhibition sets the gamma cycle. The medial septum paces theta, not gamma.

choices: Frontal cortex on both hemispheres equally
Motor cortex controlling the dominant hand
Occipital cortex processing the attended side
Occipital cortex processing the ignored side
test.explain: Alpha rises over disengaged cortex, here the region handling the ignored side. This fits the idea that alpha reflects functional inhibition.

test.q: What happens to motor-cortex beta power just after a movement ends?
choices: It falls further below baseline
It rises above baseline
It is replaced by delta waves
It shifts toward theta frequencies
test.explain: Beta drops during movement, then overshoots above baseline afterward. This overshoot is called the post-movement beta rebound.

test.q: Who recorded the first human EEG and described the alpha rhythm in 1929?
choices: Santiago Ramón y Cajal
Hans Berger
John O'Keefe
Wilder Penfield
test.explain: Hans Berger saw a roughly 10 Hz rhythm with eyes closed that was blocked by eye opening. O'Keefe is known for place cells, not the first EEG.

test.q: Which structure acts as the pacemaker for hippocampal theta?
choices: Primary visual cortex
Cerebellar vermis
Medial septum
Subthalamic nucleus
test.explain: The medial septum projects to the hippocampus and paces its theta rhythm. The subthalamic nucleus is linked to beta in Parkinson's disease.

test.q: In Parkinson's disease, which rhythm is abnormally strong in the subthalamic nucleus?
choices: Beta
Alpha
Theta
Gamma
test.explain: Dopamine loss produces excessive beta synchrony, which correlates with slowness and rigidity and falls with dopamine-replacement therapy.

test.q: Gamma bursts riding on particular phases of theta waves is an example of:
choices: Alpha blocking
Event-related desynchronization
Volume conduction
Phase-amplitude coupling
test.explain: When the phase of a slow rhythm controls the amplitude of a fast one, that is phase-amplitude coupling. Event-related desynchronization describes a drop in power during an event.

test.q: Why can scalp EEG detect brain rhythms but not single neurons?
choices: Synchronized inputs to many neurons add up
Skull bone selectively amplifies slow signals
Single neurons fire too slowly to be recorded
EEG measures blood flow rather than voltage
test.explain: One neuron's current is tiny. When thousands receive inputs in sync, their currents sum into a signal large enough to detect through the skull.

test.q: Brain rhythms are classified by their ___, measured in hertz.
test.explain: Frequency (cycles per second) defines bands such as theta, alpha, beta and gamma.

test.q: Which band (30-100 Hz) increases when a cortical area actively processes a stimulus?
test.explain: Gamma rises locally during active processing, such as in visual cortex while viewing a stimulus.

test.q: Alpha power rising over disengaged cortex supports the idea that alpha reflects functional ___.
test.explain: Alpha increases over regions that should be ignored, consistent with gating by inhibition.

kidTest.q: What are brain waves?
choices: Sounds your brain makes while you talk
Water sloshing around inside your head
Brain cells firing together in a beat
kidTest.explain: Brain waves are lots of brain cells firing together in a steady rhythm, like a crowd clapping in time.

kidTest.q: Which brain wave shows up when you close your eyes and relax?
choices: Alpha
Gamma
Beta
kidTest.explain: Alpha waves are calm waves that appear when you close your eyes and relax.

kidTest.q: When do fast gamma waves show up?
choices: When you hold your breath
When you are fast asleep
When you focus hard
kidTest.explain: Gamma waves appear when you concentrate hard on something.

kidTest.q: Theta waves help you remember...
choices: Where places are
The colors you see
The taste of food
kidTest.explain: Theta waves help you remember places, like the way to a friend's house.

kidTest.q: Doctors record brain waves with a test called an E _ _.
kidTest.explain: An EEG uses little stickers on your head to listen to your brain's beats.

advancedTest.q: Gamma peak frequency in V1 shifts with stimulus contrast (Ray and Maunsell, 2010). Why does this challenge binding-by-synchrony?
choices: Higher-contrast gamma is generated in thalamus rather than in cortex
Parts of one object at different contrasts would desynchronize
Frequency shifts show gamma arises from blood flow, not from neurons
Contrast changes abolish gamma, leaving no rhythm to synchronize
advancedTest.explain: If frequency depends on local contrast, neurons coding different parts of one object would oscillate at different frequencies. They could then not share the common clock that binding requires.

advancedTest.q: Trial-averaged beta shows a smooth, sustained change, but single trials show brief events. Which conclusion matches Shin et al. (2017)?
choices: Averaging exposes a true sustained rhythm hidden by noise
Burst rate and timing, not amplitude, track behavior
Bursts are delta waves misclassified by the band filter
Bursts are muscle artifacts that should be filtered out
advancedTest.explain: Beta occurs as transient bursts of about 150 ms whose rate and timing predicted detection. Averaging smears them into an apparently sustained rhythm, so the averaged view is the misleading one.

advancedTest.q: Gamma-band power rises while the 1/f spectral slope flattens and no spectral peak appears. The best interpretation is:
choices: An aperiodic broadband shift, not a rhythm
A genuine narrowband gamma oscillation has emerged
Volume conduction from distant theta generators
Alpha has slowed and leaked into the gamma band
advancedTest.explain: Without a peak above the aperiodic background, the power change reflects a broadband shift, possibly in E-I balance, rather than a new oscillation. Tools like specparam separate the two.

advancedTest.q: In the Lisman-Idiart theta-gamma model, what is predicted if theta slows while gamma frequency stays constant?
choices: More gamma cycles per theta cycle, so more items held
Loss of phase precession, so place cells stop firing
Fewer gamma cycles per theta cycle, so fewer items held
No change, because capacity is set by alpha power
advancedTest.explain: Capacity is set by the gamma-to-theta ratio. A longer theta cycle with unchanged gamma fits more gamma cycles, so more items can be held.

lessons.title: Intrinsic Networks: Default Mode, Salience and Frontoparietal

levels.kid:
Your brain is not one big blob doing everything the same way. Parts of it work together in teams called **networks**, even when those parts are far apart.

Three big teams:
- The **daydream team** (default mode network) gets busy when you rest, remember your last birthday, or imagine your next holiday.
- The **focus team** (frontoparietal network), near the front and top of your head, helps you solve a hard math problem.
- The **alarm team** (salience network) works like a lifeguard. It notices important things, like someone calling your name, and decides which team should take over.

When you start a hard task, the daydream team usually quiets down so the focus team can work. Scientists can see these teams even while people lie still in a brain scanner.
levels.hs:
Even when you are doing nothing, your brain is far from idle. In 1995, Bharat **Biswal** used **fMRI**, which tracks blood-oxygen changes (the **BOLD** signal) as an indirect sign of neural activity. He scanned people lying still and found that the left and right motor cortices fluctuated in sync, slowly, about once every 10 to 100 seconds. Regions whose slow signals rise and fall together are said to have **functional connectivity**. Groups of such regions form **intrinsic networks**, which scientists study with **resting-state fMRI**.

Three networks matter most for thinking:
- **Default mode network (DMN)**: the posterior cingulate cortex, medial prefrontal cortex and angular gyrus. Marcus Raichle named it in 2001 after noticing that these areas become *less* active during focused tasks. The DMN is busy during mind-wandering, recalling memories, imagining the future and thinking about other people.
- **Salience network**: the anterior insula and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex. It flags what is important right now, such as pain, a surprise or your own name.
- **Frontoparietal control network** (also called the central executive network): lateral prefrontal and posterior parietal cortex. It holds goals in mind and solves problems.

Example: you are reading, and your mind drifts to tonight's game. DMN activity rises. Then a teacher asks you a question, and the salience network helps hand control back to the frontoparietal network.
levels.college:
Resting-state fMRI measures correlations in slow (<0.1 Hz) spontaneous BOLD fluctuations. Clustering these correlations across 1,000 people, **Yeo and colleagues (2011)** split the cortex into seven reproducible networks: visual, somatomotor, dorsal attention, ventral attention/salience, limbic, frontoparietal and default. Three of these are central to cognition.

**Default mode network (DMN).** Its hubs are the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) and precuneus, the medial prefrontal cortex, the angular gyrus, the lateral temporal cortex and the hippocampal formation. It deactivates across many demanding, externally focused tasks. It activates during autobiographical memory, future simulation, self-referential judgment, theory of mind and mind-wandering.

**Salience network (SN).** Seeley and colleagues (2007) defined it around the **anterior insula** and **dorsal anterior cingulate cortex**, with links to the amygdala and ventral striatum. Both cortical hubs contain **von Economo neurons**, large spindle-shaped cells thought to support fast long-range signaling. The SN integrates bodily (interoceptive) and emotional signals to detect salient events.

**Frontoparietal control network (FPN).** It centers on the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the posterior parietal cortex along the intraparietal sulcus. It holds task rules and adapts them. Cole and colleagues described it as a **flexible hub** that shifts its connections depending on the current task. It differs from the **dorsal attention network** (frontal eye fields and intraparietal sulcus), which directs spatial attention.

Key interactions:
- **Anticorrelation**: Fox and colleagues (2005) showed that DMN activity tends to move in opposite directions to task-positive networks.
- **Switching**: the SN is proposed to toggle control between the DMN and the FPN.
- **Triple network model** (Menon, 2011): many psychiatric and neurological disorders involve disordered DMN–SN–FPN interplay.

Energy perspective: the brain uses about 20% of the body's energy at rest. Task-evoked increases add only a few percent, so intrinsic activity accounts for most of the brain's energy budget.
levels.phd:
The anticorrelation reported by Fox et al. (2005) became a cornerstone of network theory, and also a controversy. **Murphy et al. (2009)** showed that **global signal regression** (removing the whole-brain average time course) mathematically forces the correlation distribution to center near zero. This can manufacture negative correlations. Some anticorrelation survives alternative denoising, but its size depends on preprocessing. **Head motion** is a second confound: Power et al. (2012) showed that micromovements inflate short-distance correlations and weaken long-distance ones. This drove the adoption of frame censoring ("scrubbing").

The DMN is not a single entity. **Andrews-Hanna et al. (2010)** described:
- a midline core (PCC, anterior medial PFC)
- a dorsomedial subsystem (dmPFC, temporoparietal junction, temporal pole) tied to mentalizing
- a medial temporal subsystem (hippocampus, parahippocampal cortex, retrosplenial cortex) tied to memory-based simulation

In **Margulies et al. (2016)**, the principal connectivity gradient runs from primary sensorimotor cortex to the DMN. This places the DMN at the far, most abstract end of a cortical hierarchy, maximally distant from sensory input.

Evidence for causal switching comes from **Sridharan, Levitin and Menon (2008)**. Granger-causality analysis suggested that the right fronto-insular cortex drives changes in both the DMN and the FPN. This remains debated. Hemodynamic response latencies vary across regions independently of neural timing, so simulations (Smith et al., 2011) showed that lag-based methods applied to fMRI can infer the wrong causal direction.

Intracranial recordings validate the fMRI picture at fast timescales. Foster, Parvizi and colleagues found high-frequency broadband (~70–170 Hz) increases in the PCC during autobiographical recall, and suppression during arithmetic. This shows that DMN deactivation reflects reduced local population firing, not just a vascular effect.

For the FPN, Cole et al. (2013) showed that its global connectivity pattern reconfigures systematically across 64 task states. This supports **compositional coding**, in which the network flexibly combines task rules. Finally, **Seeley et al. (2009)** found that neurodegenerative syndromes map onto intrinsic networks. Alzheimer's disease targets the DMN, and behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia targets the SN. This suggests that pathology may spread along connected circuits.
levels.expert:
Group-averaged maps hide crucial individual detail. Precision functional mapping changed the field. The **Midnight Scan Club** (Gordon, Laumann et al., 2017) collected about 5 hours of resting data per person. Individual network topography proved idiosyncratic but highly stable across sessions, and reliable estimates generally need well over 30 minutes of low-motion data. Using dense sampling, **Braga and Buckner (2017)** showed that the canonical DMN splits into two parallel, interdigitated networks, **DN-A** and **DN-B**. These networks are blurred together by averaging. Terminology also varies: the "salience," "ventral attention" and "cingulo-opercular" networks overlap but are not identical.

Sample size is a second pitfall. **Marek et al. (2022)** showed that brain-wide associations between connectivity and behavior are small (typically r around 0.1). Reproducible findings require thousands of participants. Strong correlations from samples of a few dozen are likely inflated and fragile.

Clinical and surgical implications:
- **Presurgical mapping**: resting-state fMRI can localize networks in patients who cannot perform tasks, such as children, sedated patients or people with aphasia. Neurosurgeons increasingly consider network hubs, not just eloquent cortex. Damage to hubs or their white-matter links may explain cognitive decline after resections that spare classic motor and language areas.
- **Network-guided neuromodulation**: Fox et al. (2012) found that dorsolateral prefrontal TMS sites more anticorrelated with the subgenual cingulate gave better antidepressant responses. The connectivity-targeted **Stanford Neuromodulation Therapy (SNT, formerly SAINT)** received FDA clearance in 2022 for treatment-resistant depression.
- **Pharmacology**: in a precision-mapping study (Siegel et al., 2024), psilocybin caused widespread desynchronization of functional connectivity, strongest in the DMN, and several-fold larger than methylphenidate, the active control.
- **Revised maps**: Gordon et al. (2023) identified a **somato-cognitive action network** interleaved within primary motor cortex and coupled to cingulo-opercular regions. This challenges the classic homunculus.

Open questions remain. What do infraslow fluctuations compute: memory consolidation, predictive priors, or homeostatic maintenance? How do network states shift under anesthesia and sleep? Can individualized network maps become routine targets for surgery and stimulation?

keyPoints: Resting-state fMRI finds networks via correlated slow BOLD fluctuations
The DMN (PCC, mPFC, angular gyrus) supports memory, self and mind-wandering
The salience network (anterior insula, dACC) flags important events
The frontoparietal network (dlPFC, parietal cortex) is a flexible control hub
DMN and task-positive networks tend to be anticorrelated, with method caveats
Individual precision maps and large samples are reshaping network neuroscience

The effect is likely inflated and may not replicate

Individual networks shift location from hour to hour

choices: Insula lesions tend to improve task switching in patients
The insula is silent during most cognitive tasks studied

advancedTest.explain: Hemodynamic latencies vary between regions independently of neural timing, so lag-based methods on fMRI can infer the wrong causal direction.

lessons.title: Predictive Coding and the Bayesian Brain

levels.kid:
Your brain is a super guesser. Before you even look or listen, it is already guessing what will happen next.

Think about a song you know well. When it plays, you can sing the next words before they come. Your brain does this with everything: sights, sounds and touches.

When the guess is right, the brain stays calm. When the guess is wrong, that is a **surprise**! The brain pays extra attention to surprises and fixes its guess for next time.

This is also why you can't tickle yourself. Your brain knows exactly where your fingers will go, so the touch is no surprise.

When something is blurry or hard to see, your brain uses what it has learned before to make its best guess.
levels.hs:
For a long time, people pictured the brain as a camera: light comes in, and the brain builds a picture from scratch. **Predictive coding** turns this around. It proposes that the brain is constantly predicting its own sensory input and mainly processes the part it got wrong.

Key terms:
- **Prediction**: the brain's guess about what the senses are about to report.
- **Prediction error**: the gap between the guess and what actually arrives. This is the 'news' that updates the brain's model.
- **Prior**: what you already believe before new evidence comes in, based on past experience.

The idea is old. In the 1860s, Hermann von **Helmholtz** called perception 'unconscious inference.' Today it is often described using **Bayes' rule**, a formula for combining a prior belief with new evidence. That is why people call it the **Bayesian brain**.

A real example is the **hollow-face illusion**. When you look at the inside of a mask, it seems to pop outward like a normal face. Your prior that faces are convex is so strong that it overrides the depth cues from your eyes.

Predictions also explain why you can't tickle yourself. Your brain predicts the feel of your own fingers and turns the signal down. Surprises, not predictable events, get the strongest response.
levels.college:
Predictive coding frames perception as **inference**: the brain must guess the hidden causes of noisy, ambiguous sensory signals.

**Bayes' rule** gives the ideal recipe. The **posterior** (belief after evidence) is proportional to the **likelihood** (how well a cause explains the data) times the **prior** (belief before the data). Priors explain many illusions. A shaded disk looks like a bump or a dent depending on its shading because the visual system assumes **light comes from above**.

**The hierarchical scheme.** In predictive coding, cortex is organized as a hierarchy:
- Higher areas send **predictions** down to lower areas through feedback connections.
- Lower areas compare the prediction with incoming input and send the **prediction error** up through feedforward connections.
- Higher areas adjust their model to reduce the error. When predictions are good, little error remains, which is metabolically efficient.

**Precision weighting.** Not all errors deserve equal trust. **Precision** is the inverse of variance, a measure of reliability. Errors from reliable signals are amplified, and errors from noisy signals are discounted. **Attention** is proposed to work by turning up the gain on chosen prediction errors.

**The brain combines cues like an ideal observer.** Ernst and Banks (2002) had people judge an object's height by sight and touch. The brain weighted each cue in proportion to its reliability (inverse variance), and the combined estimate was more precise than either cue alone, as Bayes predicts. When the researchers degraded the visual cue, reliance shifted toward touch.

**Neural signatures of surprise.**
- **Mismatch negativity (MMN)**: an EEG response peaking roughly 100-250 ms after a rare 'deviant' tone embedded among repeated 'standard' tones, even when the listener ignores the sounds.
- **Self-generated sensation**: Blakemore, Wolpert and Frith showed that self-produced touch feels weaker because a copy of the motor command (an **efference copy**) predicts and cancels its sensory consequences.
levels.phd:
Formal predictive coding was crystallized by **Rao and Ballard (1999)**. They trained a hierarchical network in which each level predicted the activity of the level below and passed up residual errors. The model reproduced **extra-classical receptive field** effects such as end-stopping. A V1-like unit responds less to a line extending beyond its receptive field because higher levels, having learned that lines continue, predict it away.

**Friston** generalized the idea into the **free-energy principle**: organisms minimize variational free energy, an upper bound on surprise (negative log model evidence). Perception reduces free energy by updating beliefs; **active inference** reduces it by acting to make sensations match predictions. Critics note that a principle this general is hard to falsify, so the testable content lies in specific process models.

**Canonical microcircuit.** Bastos et al. (2012) mapped predictive coding onto laminar anatomy. Superficial pyramidal cells (layers 2/3) carry prediction errors forward, while deep pyramidal cells (layers 5/6) carry predictions backward. Feedforward signalling is associated with gamma-band activity and feedback with alpha/beta.

**Suppression or sharpening?** Expected stimuli usually evoke smaller responses (**expectation suppression**). Summerfield et al. (2008) showed that fMRI repetition suppression in face-selective cortex is larger when repetitions are probable, implicating prediction rather than pure neural fatigue. Kok, Jehee and de Lange (2012) found that expected gratings produced lower V1 BOLD yet more decodable orientation patterns. Expectation seems to **sharpen** the representation by silencing neurons inconsistent with the prediction.

**Error neurons?** In mouse V1, Keller and colleagues found neurons that fire when visual flow fails to match running speed (visuomotor mismatch). However, many oddball responses can be explained by **stimulus-specific adaptation (SSA)**. The **many-standards control** presents the deviant tone equally rarely amid varied tones. A deviant response exceeding this control indicates genuine prediction error. Parras et al. (2017) used such controls and found prediction error signals growing from auditory midbrain to cortex.

**Bayesian observers.** Weiss, Simoncelli and Adelson (2002) explained motion illusions, such as low-contrast stimuli appearing slower, as optimal inference under a prior favouring slow speeds. Skeptics (Jones and Love; Bowers and Davis) argue that flexible priors can fit almost any data after the fact.
levels.expert:
For clinician-scientists, predictive processing is most useful as a framework for **computational psychiatry and neurology**, where symptoms are modelled as faulty belief updating.

**Psychosis.** Reduced MMN amplitude is one of the most replicated findings in schizophrenia. The NMDA antagonist ketamine reduces MMN in healthy volunteers, linking glutamatergic signalling to error computation. Accounts split symptoms by level: delusions as aberrantly precise low-level errors that demand explanation (Corlett, Fletcher), and hallucinations as overweighted priors. Powers, Mathys and Corlett (2017) paired lights with tones until participants reported hearing tones that were absent. Voice-hearers were more susceptible, and a **hierarchical Gaussian filter** model attributed this to overweighting priors relative to sensory input.

**Neuromodulators as precision.** Pharmacology maps onto the framework:
- **Acetylcholine**: proposed to signal expected uncertainty, boosting sensory precision (Yu and Dayan, 2005).
- **Noradrenaline**: unexpected uncertainty, prompting model updating or resets.
- **Dopamine**: reward prediction error (covered in the reward unit) and, in active inference, precision over action policies.
- **5-HT2A agonists (psychedelics)**: the REBUS model proposes they relax the precision of high-level priors.
These are hypotheses with partial support, not established mechanisms.

**Neurology.** Functional neurological disorder is modelled as abnormally precise priors about the body that drive genuine movements or sensations without a structural lesion, explaining distractibility and why attention worsens symptoms (Edwards et al., 2012). Placebo analgesia and chronic pain are framed as expectations shaping nociceptive inference. Phantom limb pain fits a body model that persists after amputation; mirror therapy may supply corrective visual evidence.

**Pitfalls.**
- Oddball effects in EEG or ECoG need adaptation controls before invoking prediction error.
- A well-fitting Bayesian model shows behaviour is consistent with Bayes, not that neurons compute posteriors.
- 'Precision' can explain opposite findings unless parameters are constrained in advance.

**Open questions.** Are predictions and errors carried by distinct cell types, such as VIP and SST interneuron circuits, or by the same neurons in different states? How are priors learned and stored across timescales? Intracranial recordings in epilepsy and awake neurosurgery patients increasingly test laminar and timing predictions directly in humans.

keyPoints: The brain constantly predicts its sensory input and processes mainly the prediction error
Bayes' rule: posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior
Predictions flow down the cortical hierarchy; errors flow up
Precision (inverse variance) weights errors; attention may boost precision
Mismatch negativity and weak self-tickle are classic signatures of prediction
Clinical models link faulty priors and precision to psychosis and functional disorders

test.q: In predictive coding, what does a prediction error signal represent?
choices: The brain's best guess before any input
The delay before a signal reaches cortex
The overall strength of the sensory input
The gap between expected and actual input
test.explain: A prediction error is the mismatch between what the brain predicted and what arrived. The brain's guess itself is the prediction, not the error.

test.q: According to Bayes' rule, the posterior is proportional to:
choices: The likelihood divided by the prior
The likelihood times the prior
The prior plus the prediction error
The prior minus the likelihood
test.explain: Bayes' rule multiplies the likelihood (how well a cause explains the data) by the prior (belief before the data).

test.q: In the hierarchical predictive coding scheme, which way do predictions mainly travel?
choices: Downward from higher to lower areas
Upward from sensory to higher areas
Sideways within one cortical area
Outward from cortex to the brainstem
test.explain: Predictions are sent down by feedback connections; prediction errors travel up by feedforward connections.

test.q: In Ernst and Banks's experiment, how did the brain combine sight and touch?
choices: By which cue reached cortex first
By which sense evolved earlier
By how reliable each cue was
By how recently each cue arrived
test.explain: Each cue was weighted by its reliability (inverse variance), and the combined estimate was more precise than either cue alone.

test.q: Why does self-produced touch feel weaker than the same touch from someone else?
choices: Touch receptors adapt within milliseconds
Your own fingers have weaker nerve endings
The brain predicts and dampens the touch
Self-touch is blocked in the spinal cord
test.explain: An efference copy of the motor command predicts the sensory result and cancels much of it, so there is little surprise.

test.q: The mismatch negativity (MMN) is evoked by:
choices: A loud tone after a long silence
A long series of identical tones
Two different tones played together
A rare tone among repeated tones
test.explain: MMN appears when a rare deviant breaks a pattern of repeated standards, even when the listener ignores the sounds.

test.q: In predictive coding, attention is proposed to work by:
choices: Turning up the gain on chosen errors
Blocking feedforward sensory signals
Slowing down the brain's alpha rhythm
Deleting priors held by higher areas
test.explain: Attention is modelled as increasing the precision (gain) of selected prediction errors so they have more influence on beliefs.

test.q: The hollow-face illusion, where the inside of a mask seems to pop outward, demonstrates:
choices: The two eyes send conflicting images
Faces are stored in short-term memory
A strong prior that faces are convex
Depth perception fails in dim light
test.explain: The prior that faces bulge outward is so strong that it overrides the depth cues from the eyes.

test.q: A shaded disk can look like a bump or a dent depending on its shading. This happens because the visual system assumes:
choices: Surfaces are usually seen head-on
Light usually comes from above
Objects are usually far away
Objects usually move slowly
test.explain: The light-from-above prior makes top-lit disks look convex. A slow-speed prior exists too, but it explains motion illusions, not shading.

test.q: Which 19th-century scientist described perception as 'unconscious inference'?
test.explain: Hermann von Helmholtz proposed in the 1860s that perception is an inference about the causes of sensations.

test.q: In Bayesian terms, the brain's belief before seeing new evidence is called the ___.
test.explain: The prior is the belief held before new data, based on past experience.

test.q: The reliability of a signal, defined as the inverse of its variance, is called ___.
test.explain: Precision weights prediction errors: reliable signals count more, noisy ones less.

kidTest.q: What does your brain do all the time, according to this idea?
choices: Makes guesses about what comes next
Sleeps until something loud happens
Saves each sound it hears in a list
kidTest.explain: Your brain is always guessing what will happen next.

kidTest.q: What does the brain pay the most attention to?
choices: Things that happen the same each day
Surprises that break its guess
Sounds that are soft and very quiet
kidTest.explain: Surprises tell the brain its guess was wrong, so it pays extra attention and fixes the guess.

kidTest.q: Why can't you tickle yourself?
choices: Your brain knows the touch is coming
Your fingers are too warm to tickle
Your skin is too thick in that spot
kidTest.explain: Your brain predicts exactly where your fingers will go, so the touch is no surprise.

kidTest.q: When something is blurry, what helps your brain make its best guess?
choices: How loud the room is
How tired your eyes feel
What it has learned before
kidTest.explain: The brain uses what it learned in the past to guess what a blurry thing is.

kidTest.q: When the brain's guess is wrong, that is called a s _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: A wrong guess is a surprise, and the brain uses it to update its guess for next time.

advancedTest.q: Kok et al. (2012) found that expected gratings evoked lower V1 BOLD yet more decodable orientation patterns. The best interpretation is:
choices: Expectation sharpens the code, silencing mismatched cells
Expected stimuli are routed past V1 to prefrontal cortex
The BOLD signal saturates and hides predictable activity
Expectation lowers attention so fewer neurons respond
advancedTest.explain: Lower overall activity with better decoding fits sharpening: neurons inconsistent with the prediction are suppressed, leaving a cleaner pattern. Reduced attention would be expected to worsen decoding, not improve it.

advancedTest.q: A deviant tone evokes a larger response than the same tone presented equally rarely in a many-standards control. This indicates:
choices: Habituation of the whole auditory pathway
A loudness artifact of the deviant tone itself
Pure adaptation of neurons tuned to the standard
Genuine prediction error beyond simple adaptation
advancedTest.explain: The many-standards control matches the deviant's rarity, so it accounts for stimulus-specific adaptation. Any extra response reflects violation of a pattern, which is prediction error.

advancedTest.q: In a cue-combination task, the visual estimate has one quarter the variance of the touch estimate. An ideal Bayesian observer will:
choices: Rely on vision and discard touch
Weight touch more to correct vision
Weight the two cues equally
Favor vision 4:1 with lower variance
advancedTest.explain: Weights are proportional to inverse variance, so vision gets four times the weight. The combined estimate is more precise than either cue alone, so touch is still used rather than discarded.

advancedTest.q: In Powers et al.'s conditioned hallucination task, voice-hearers more often reported tones that were not played. Computational modelling attributed this to:
choices: Weaker attention to the visual cue
Faster forgetting of light-tone pairings
Overweighting priors relative to input
Unusually sharp hearing for faint tones
advancedTest.explain: The hierarchical Gaussian filter fits showed stronger reliance on learned light-tone expectations than on sensory evidence. Faster forgetting of the pairings would reduce false tone reports, not increase them.
